title: How to automate proposals and save time in your workflow
summary: Learn how to automate proposals with templates, e-signatures, and follow-ups so you spend less time drafting and more time closing deals.
body_markdown:
Chasing down client details, reformatting the same document for the tenth time, and refreshing your inbox to see if a proposal got opened all eat into hours you could spend on billable work. If you're still building every proposal from scratch, you're not alone, but it's one of the easiest parts of a freelance or small agency workflow to fix. Learning how to automate proposals means setting up templates, client data, e-signatures, and follow-ups to run with less manual effort, so you spend less time on paperwork and more time closing deals. This guide walks through each phase of that process, building on the fundamentals covered in our complete guide to business proposals for small businesses, so you can turn a repetitive task into a repeatable system.

## Map out your proposal process before you automate


Before you automate anything, write down every step you currently take to send a proposal. Most freelancers repeat the same manual tasks each time: drafting scope language from memory, reformatting an old document, calculating pricing by hand, and emailing a PDF before following up blind. These repetitive, low-judgment steps are the safest to hand off first, while anything requiring client-specific judgment stays manual for now. This same audit approach works well if you're learning how to automate sales more broadly, not just proposals.


### Manual vs. automated proposal steps


Task Manual approach Automated approach


Drafting scope and structure Rewriting from an old file each time Reusable, on-brand template


Client and pricing details Copy-pasting from email threads Auto-populated from saved records


Sending for approval Printing, signing, scanning Secure e-signature link


Tracking engagement Guessing based on silence Automated open and view tracking


## Automate proposals with reusable, on-brand templates


Once you know which steps are repetitive, templates are usually one of the quickest wins. Instead of starting from a blank page or digging up an old file, a saved template gives you a consistent structure to fill in, which can help cut down drafting time. If you want a refresher on what a strong proposal actually needs before you template it, our guide on how to write a proposal covers the core sections worth keeping.


### Build templates by service or project type


A single generic template rarely fits every client. Build separate versions for each core offer instead, such as a website redesign, a monthly retainer, or a one-off consulting package, so the scope language and pricing structure already match the type of work.


### Keep branding consistent automatically


Save your colors, logo, and layout once so proposals can look polished without manual reformatting. This keeps client-facing documents consistent even when you're sending several a week.


## Auto-populate client and pricing details


Templates handle the structure, but retyping client names and pricing line by line still eats time. Pulling those details from saved records instead of old email threads cuts down on copy-paste errors that can slow down client approvals.


### Pull client details from your CRM records


A[CRM](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/crm/) , or customer relationship management tool, stores client and company details you'd otherwise dig up from old threads. Populating a proposal from saved records means names, contacts, and company info are accurate without retyping.


### Automate itemized pricing with taxes and discounts


Itemized pricing tables can calculate per-line taxes and apply fixed or percentage discounts automatically, so totals can stay accurate without manual math.


## Streamline e-signatures and approvals


Once a client is ready to say yes, printing, signing, and scanning a proposal only slows things down. E-signature workflows let clients approve a proposal from a secure link, which can help reduce the back-and-forth that comes with paper-based approvals. Keeping a full audit trail of signer identity, IP address, and timestamps also gives you a clear record of who approved what and when.


### Send proposals for signature via secure link


Instead of attaching a document to an email, clients can sign from any device through a secure magic link, with no password to manage. This works well alongside[Bonsai contracts](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/contracts/) , where the same signing flow carries over once a proposal turns into a formal agreement.


### Set up multi-signer workflows for bigger deals


Larger projects often need more than one signature, whether that's a client-side stakeholder and a procurement contact, or a co-founder signing alongside you. Multi-signer workflows let each person add an independent signature to the same document, so approvals don't get stuck waiting on a single inbox.

## Automate follow-ups and engagement tracking


Guessing when to follow up usually means either chasing a client too soon or waiting too long after interest has faded. Automated view tracking removes that guesswork by showing you exactly when engagement happens.


### Know when a client opens your proposal


A notification triggers the moment a client opens the document, so you know it landed instead of wondering if it's stuck in a spam folder.


### Time your follow-up around engagement data


Use that open activity to decide when to send a follow-up email or book a call, rather than reaching out on a fixed schedule. Pairing this timing with a strong follow-up message, like the approach in how to write a sales proposal that wins clients, keeps outreach relevant instead of repetitive. It also helps you avoid chasing clients who haven't opened the proposal yet.


## Turn accepted proposals into contracts and invoices automatically


Once a client accepts a proposal, re-typing the same scope and pricing into a new document just adds another chance for errors. Connecting proposals to contracts and billing means that acceptance step triggers the next one automatically, instead of starting a fresh document from scratch.


### Convert an accepted proposal into an invoice


When a client signs off, the accepted proposal's line items can generate an invoice directly, with no manual re-entry of scope, pricing, or client details. That invoice then flows into[Bonsai invoicing](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/invoicing/) , where it's ready to send without rebuilding it from a separate template.


### Link contracts and invoices to one client record


Keeping contracts and their related invoices tied to a single client record can help reduce time spent hunting across email threads and folders to confirm what was agreed to and what's been billed. It can also help reduce duplicate data entry between sales and billing, since both steps pull from the same source instead of separate files.


## Test and refine your automated proposal workflow


Automating your proposal process isn't a one-time setup. Check which templates lead to signed deals and which ones stall, and ask recent clients what felt clear or confusing. Update pricing tables and scope language as your services or rates change, so templates never fall out of date. If the whole process feels overwhelming, automate one step at a time, starting with templates or e-signatures, rather than overhauling everything at once. Small, steady adjustments keep the system working for you instead of against you.

None of this replaces judgment on scope or pricing, but it removes the repetitive parts, drafting, data entry, and manual tracking, so more of the week goes toward the client work that actually pays.


## FAQ


### **Q1: What should every automated proposal include?**


An automated proposal should still include the same core elements as any strong proposal: a clear scope of work, itemized pricing, timeline, and terms for approval. What changes with automation is how those elements get built. Instead of writing scope language from scratch each time, a saved template holds the structure, and client details and pricing pull in from existing records rather than getting retyped.


Beyond the document itself, an automated workflow should also cover what happens after you hit send. That means a way to see when a client opens the proposal and a signature process that does not require printing or scanning. Together, these pieces turn a proposal from a one-off document into a repeatable process you can run for new clients.


### **Q2: Is proposal automation worth it for freelancers and small agencies?**


For most freelancers and small agencies, proposal automation is worth exploring because it targets the repetitive parts of the process, drafting, data entry, and manual tracking, rather than the judgment calls that still need a human. Freeing up that time can support more consistent proposal quality even as the number of proposals you send increases.


The value tends to scale with proposal volume. A freelancer sending one proposal a month may not notice much difference, but someone sending several a week often finds that templates, auto-populated details, and tracking add up to meaningful time savings. The right approach depends on how much of your week currently goes into rebuilding documents by hand.


### **Q3: Can AI help you automate proposals faster?**


AI-assisted writing tools can help draft scope language or suggest wording for a proposal, which can speed up the initial drafting step for some freelancers. That said, AI-generated language still needs a human review pass to make sure pricing, scope, and terms accurately reflect the actual project.


AI is generally better suited to drafting support than to the rest of the proposal workflow, such as pulling accurate client records, calculating itemized pricing, or managing e-signatures. Those steps are typically handled more reliably through templates and connected client data than through AI generation alone. Combining both approaches, AI for early drafts and structured tools for the rest, tends to work better than relying on either one exclusively.


### **Q4: Are there free ways to automate proposals?**


Yes, there are some free ways to start automating proposals, even without dedicated software. Saving a reusable document template in a word processor or slide tool removes the need to rebuild scope language from scratch, and a simple spreadsheet can help you track which proposals are still awaiting a response.


Free approaches tend to hit a ceiling once volume increases, since manual templates still require copying in client details by hand and offer no built-in way to know when a proposal has been opened. For freelancers sending only a handful of proposals a month, a free template-based system may be enough. For those sending proposals more frequently, dedicated proposal software often reduces more of the manual work.


### **Q5: How does Bonsai help with automating proposals?**

When a client accepts a proposal, Bonsai generates an invoice from the proposal's line items without manual re-entry, and Zoom meeting transcripts can sync to the client's record so scoping call notes and proposal history stay together. A freelancer sending several proposals a week can use this to cut down on repetitive drafting and data entry, while still handling the scope and pricing decisions that require personal judgment.


That combination is what makes proposal automation practical for freelancers and small agencies juggling multiple clients at once.


Turning proposal work into a repeatable system does not require overhauling your entire process overnight. Start with the step that costs you the most time each week, whether that is rebuilding a template or chasing down a signature, and let the rest follow as your workflow settles in. Bonsai by Zoom supports templates, client data, e-signatures, and follow-up tracking, while Zoom Meetings handles the client calls that go alongside this work, so proposals take less effort to send and less guesswork to manage.
